newsitem.title: GREECE: EU, OSCE review peacekeeping deployment to Albania.
newsitem.headline: EU, OSCE review peacekeeping deployment to Albania.

text.p: Representatives from the European Union and the Organisation for European Security and Cooperation will meet Albanian Prime Minister Bashkim Fino on Thursday to review deployment of peace-keepers in lawless Albania.

Fino was scheduled to meet Dutch Foreign Minister Hans van Mierlo, current president of the EU general affairs council, and former Austrian chancellor Franz Vranitzky, the special OSCE envoy for Albania at the Greek Foreign Ministry.

"The three guests and (Greek) Foreign Minister Theodoros Pangalos will meet to review the distribution of aid and the stationing of the U.N.-approved force to Albania," a senior government official told Reuters.
"The chaos in Albania must be contained immediately if we want lasting peace in the Balkans."

Fino arrived on Wednesday on a two-day visit and held long talks with Prime Minister Costas Simitis. Senior ministers from his all-party government will hold separate talks with their Greek counterparts on Thursday.

"The Albanian delegation is here for help. This is what Fino told Simitis and this is what he'll tell Van Mierlo and Vranitzky. They need everything from money to food and specialists to restructure their shattered state machine," the official said.

Fino said after the meeting with Simitis that he secured an $80 million loan from Greece and welcomed the participation of Greek peace-keepers in a U.N.-approved force to help restore order in Albania.
"We secured a credit of about $80 million which is quite good. We also asked the Greek government to help us (organise) with specialists June's elections," Fino said.
Fino, 34, was appointed to head a unity government after an armed revolt in southern Albania.

Italy will lead the force of about 5,000 men, which Rome says could start deployment about April 12. Fino met early on Wednesday with Italian Prime Minister Romano Prodi in the southern Albanian town of Gjirokaster.
Designed to secure the distribution of humanitarian aid in the impoverished country, the force will try to secure the ports of Durres and Vlore and Tirana airport.
So far Italy is expected to provide 2,000 to 2,500 troops, France 1,000, Greece 700, Turkey 500, Spain 500 and Romania 400.
"The multinational force will secure the (distribution) of humanitarian aid at the (Tirana) airport, the main ports and roads," Fino said.
Athens has been closely monitoring the effects of last month's insurrection on the large Greek minority living in the south, much of which is in rebel hands.
It is also worried violence and economic disaster in the former communist state could send a new wave of illegal Albanian immigrants across its rugged border.
Hundreds of thousands of illegal foreign workers, mostly the result of an Albanian refugee influx after the fall of communism in 1990, are already taxing its fragile economy.
"The number of illegal immigrants crossing to Greece must be confined," Simitis said.

Prompted by the collapse of popular pyramid savings schemes which left thousands destitute, the revolt has left the south lawless for weeks, with groups armed with weapons looted from army depots roaming the area.

Rebel committees controlling southern towns say they are trying to stop the banditry and looting that has killed scores of people but demand the resignation of President Sali Berisha, blaming him for the collapse of the investment schemes.
Berisha has refused to step down but was forced to appoint Fino, a socialist, to head a 10-party unity government until elections, expected in June.
